related_questions.question: How do you get diagnosed with diabetes?

text_blocks.snippet: Diabetes is diagnosed through blood tests that measure blood glucose levels. A health care professional can diagnose diabetes, prediabetes, and gestational diabetes through these tests. If blood glucose levels are higher than normal, it can indicate diabetes. There are several tests used, including A1C tests, fasting blood glucose tests, and oral glucose tolerance tests.
snippet_highlighted_words: through blood tests that measure blood glucose levels

list.title: A1C Test:
list.snippet: This test provides an average of blood glucose levels over the past 2-3 months. An A1C of 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes, while 5.7% to 6.4% suggests prediabetes.

list.title: Fasting Blood Glucose Test:
list.snippet: This test measures blood glucose levels after an overnight fast (no food or drinks except water for at least 8 hours). A fasting blood glucose level of 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.

list.title: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT):
list.snippet: This test measures blood glucose levels before and after drinking a sugary liquid. A two-hour blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: While some individuals with prediabetes or diabetes may experience symptoms like increased thirst, urination, or unexplained weight loss, others may not have noticeable symptoms.

list.title: Prediabetes:
list.snippet: Prediabetes is a condition where blood glucose levels are higher than normal but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes.

list.title: Early Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Early diagnosis and management of diabetes are crucial to prevent or delay complications.
It's essential to consult with a healthcare professional for accurate diagnosis and personalized treatment recommendations.
Self-diagnosis using over-the-counter blood glucose meters is not recommended.
If you have questions or concerns about your diagnosis, discuss them with your doctor or healthcare team.

related_questions.snippet: The three Ps are the most common signs of diabetes. Polyuria means frequent urination, polydipsia means excessive thirst, and polyphagia means excessive hunger. text_blocks.snippet: Common signs of diabetes include increased thirst and urination, increased hunger, fatigue, blurry vision, slow-healing sores, and tingling or numbness in hands or feet. Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes share many of these symptoms, though Type 1 symptoms often appear more quickly and intensely. It's important to consult a doctor if you experience any of these signs, especially if you have risk factors for diabetes.
snippet_highlighted_words: increased thirst and urination, increased hunger, fatigue, blurry vision, slow-healing sores, and tingling or numbness in hands or feet

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the symptoms:

list.title: Increased Thirst (Polydipsia):
list.snippet: When blood sugar is high, your kidneys work harder to filter and remove it, leading to increased urination and dehydration, which causes thirst.

list.title: Increased Urination (Polyuria):
list.snippet: Frequent urination, especially at night, is a common sign as your body tries to flush out excess sugar.

list.title: Increased Hunger (Polyphagia):
list.snippet: Even after eating, you might feel hungry because your body isn't effectively using glucose for energy.

list.title: Fatigue:
list.snippet: High blood sugar levels can interfere with your body's ability to convert food into energy, leading to feeling tired and weak.

list.title: Blurred Vision:
list.snippet: High blood sugar can affect the lens of your eye, causing blurry vision.

list.title: Slow-healing Sores and Cuts:
list.snippet: High blood sugar can impair your body's ability to heal, making minor injuries take longer to recover.

list.title: Tingling or Numbness:
list.snippet: Diabetic neuropathy, nerve damage caused by high blood sugar, can lead to tingling, numbness, or pain in your extremities, especially your hands and feet.

list.title: Unexplained Weight Loss:
list.snippet: Especially noticeable in Type 1 diabetes, this occurs because your body starts burning fat and muscle for energy when it can't use glucose.

list.title: Frequent Infections:
list.snippet: High blood sugar can weaken your immune system, making you more susceptible to infections like urinary tract infections, skin infections, or yeast infections.

list.title: Darkened Skin:
list.snippet: Skin darkening, particularly in the folds of your body like the neck, groin, and armpits, can be a sign.

list.title: Type 1 vs. Type 2:
list.snippet: Type 1 diabetes symptoms tend to appear more quickly and dramatically than Type 2 symptoms, which can develop gradually and may be mild or even unnoticeable in the early stages.

list.title: Gestational Diabetes:
list.snippet: High blood sugar during pregnancy (gestational diabetes) may not always have noticeable symptoms, but it's important to get screened by your doctor, especially if you have risk factors.

list.title: Early Detection:
list.snippet: If you experience any of these symptoms, especially if you have risk factors for diabetes (like being overweight, having a family history of diabetes, or being over 45), it's crucial to see a doctor for testing and diagnosis.
